\chapter{The Word That Carries a Thought}
\label{ch:gu-that-clause}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I think and what I know, hand a whole sentence to a verb with ke, and say plainly that I do not know.}

The complementiser. ane and pan set two sentences side by side; ke puts one INSIDE another, which is what a verb of thinking or knowing needs before it can be given anything to think or know. vicharvu and jaanvu were both taught twenty-nine chapters ago and neither has ever had an object; both get one here, and jaanto nathi supplies the flat I-do-not-know that sits beside chapter 35s I-do-not-understand.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ke]{\gu{કે} (ke) — that}

\label{lesson:GU-C33-ke}



\begin{quote}
One chapter back: the word that sets one clause against another. Two chapters back, at the head of the repair chapter: the word that replaces \emph{chhe}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{paṇ}, then \emph{nathī}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The joining words so far put two sentences \textbf{side by side}. \textbf{\gu{કે}} does something different: it lets one sentence be \textbf{swallowed by} another, as the thing a verb is about.

\begin{quote}
\emph{(verb of thinking or knowing)} \textbf{\gu{કે}} \emph{(whole sentence)}
\end{quote}

English does the same with \emph{that} — \textquotedblleft{}I know \textbf{that} it is late\textquotedblright{} — and, like English, Gujarati often lets it drop in speech. Learn it in place first.

\textbf{\gu{કે}} is not a stranger. It is the old \textbf{k-} stem that also starts \textbf{\gu{કેમ}} (\emph{why}) — the same handful of sounds does the asking and the reporting, and that stem has more work to do before this run of chapters is finished.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ke}, and hear how little it is. It carries an entire sentence.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} two sentences joined by \emph{ane}, then one swallowed by \emph{ke}.
  \item \emph{Build:} any sentence you can say, with \emph{ke} in front of it, waiting.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\gu{કે}} do that \textbf{\gu{અને}} cannot? (\emph{ane} sets two sentences side by side; \emph{ke} puts one \textbf{inside} the other.) What other word does its \textbf{k-} begin? (\emph{kem}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vichārũ chhũ ke]{\gu{વિચારું} \gu{છું} \gu{કે} (vichārũ chhũ ke) — I think that…}

\label{lesson:GU-C33-vichaarun-ke}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, the swallowing word. And from the verb chapter, long behind you, the verb \textbf{to think}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ke}, and \emph{vichārvũ}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{વિચારું} \gu{છું} \gu{કે} …} — \emph{vichārũ chhũ ke …} — \textquotedblleft{}I think that …\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three pieces, and two of them are old. \textbf{\gu{વિચારું}} is the verb with the ending that means \emph{I}; \textbf{\gu{છું}} is the \emph{am} you have had since the second chapter; \textbf{\gu{કે}} opens the space where your opinion goes.

Everything you can already say can now be said \textbf{as an opinion} rather than as a fact, by putting it after \textbf{\gu{કે}} and nothing else. That is a large change for one small word, and it is the difference between reporting the world and having a view about it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
An A1 speaker who can only state facts sounds like a list. The frame above is what turns a list into a conversation — and it is also how you soften a disagreement, because \emph{I think that it is not so} lands very differently from \emph{it is not so}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vichārũ chhũ ke …} and finish it with any sentence you own.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the bare sentence, then the same inside the frame.
  \item \emph{Build:} an opinion whose inside half is negative.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give an opinion about anything you can name. Which of the three pieces was new today? (Only the way they combine — \textbf{\gu{કે}} came last lesson and the other two are chapters old.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ke]{\gu{કે} reaches the page}

\label{lesson:GU-C33-ke-write}



\begin{quote}
Say the swallowing word. Then a long reach back, to a word taught many chapters ago and not asked for since: what is \textbf{\gu{શાળા}}?

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{shāḷā} — school
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — two signs, neither new}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ક}} — \emph{ka} · \textbf{\gu{ે}} — the \emph{e} stroke
\end{quote}

Uncover \textbf{\gu{કે}} and name both pieces. Like \textbf{\gu{અને}} last chapter, this word costs the hand nothing it did not already have.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Copy \textbf{\gu{કે}} once with the model in view. Then write \textbf{\gu{અને}} beside it from memory and compare the two \textbf{\gu{ે}} strokes: the same sign, sitting on different letters.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textbf{\gu{કે}} from memory. Which stroke does it share with \textbf{\gu{અને}}? (The \textbf{\gu{ે}} above.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jāṇũ chhũ ke]{\gu{જાણું} \gu{છું} \gu{કે} (jāṇũ chhũ ke) — I know that…}

\label{lesson:GU-C33-jaanun-ke}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back you wrote it. And from the verb chapter: \textbf{to know}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\gu{કે}}, and \emph{jāṇvũ}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જાણું} \gu{છું} \gu{કે} …} — \emph{jāṇũ chhũ ke …} — \textquotedblleft{}I know that …\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The same shape as the thinking frame, with a different verb in front. That is the point of \textbf{\gu{કે}}: it does not care which verb precedes it.

\textbf{\gu{જાણવું}} and English \textbf{know} are the same ancient word — the \emph{gnō-} that also gives \emph{knowledge}, \emph{diagnosis} and \emph{ignore}. The kinship has been true since the verb chapter; what is new is that the verb finally has something to take.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: and the half you need more}]
Negate it with the word from two chapters back and you get the sentence a traveller actually uses:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જાણતો} \gu{નથી}} — \emph{jāṇto nathī} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I don't know}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

As with \emph{samajto nathī}, the \textbf{-\gu{તો}} is masculine and \textbf{-\gu{તી}} feminine: a woman says \emph{jāṇtī nathī}. Said alone, without any \textbf{\gu{કે}} after it, this is a complete and very common reply.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jāṇũ chhũ ke …} with any sentence after it.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jāṇto nathī} — or \emph{jāṇtī nathī} — flat, as a whole answer.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{samajto nathī} and \emph{jāṇto nathī}. Two different admissions.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{I don't know}. Then say \emph{I don't understand}. What is the difference you are drawing? (Not having the fact, against not having followed.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The reporting frames, all together}

\label{lesson:GU-C33-ke-checkpoint}



\begin{quote}
No new words. One run through what \textbf{\gu{કે}} made possible.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{કે}} — the word that puts a whole sentence \textbf{inside} another.
  \item \textbf{\gu{વિચારું} \gu{છું} \gu{કે} …} — an opinion rather than a fact.
  \item \textbf{\gu{જાણું} \gu{છું} \gu{કે} …} — and, negated, \emph{jāṇto nathī}, \textquotedblleft{}I don't know\textquotedblright{}.
  \item \textbf{\gu{કે}} on the page, on two signs that were already yours.
\end{itemize}

Two chapters ago you could not say \emph{and}. You can now hand an entire sentence to a verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} an opinion, then the same content as a thing you know.
  \item \emph{Build:} one sentence using \emph{ane}, and one using \emph{paṇ}, from the chapter before.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jāṇto nathī}, flat, at conversational speed.
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\gu{કે}} and \textbf{\gu{અને}} side by side, naming the shared stroke.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give an opinion, then admit you do not know something. Next chapter: the answer to a question this book has been able to ask since chapter 3 and never able to answer — \textbf{why}.
\end{tcolorbox}
